newsitem.title: USA: AOL, CompuServe, Prodigy settle U.S. charges.
newsitem.headline: AOL, CompuServe, Prodigy settle U.S. charges.

text.p: America Online, CompuServe and Prodigy Services Thursday settled government allegations that supposed "free trial" offers resulted in unexpected charges to consumers.

The Federal Trade Commission voted 5-0 for the agreement requiring that -- among other things -- companies get written authorization from consumers before the companies tap their checking accounts electronically.
No fines were levied against the three.
However, AOL must prepare a consumer education program about the use of electronic payment systems. It will be distributed through the Web and 50,000 color brochures.
The government said one problem was that the firms would offer introductory free service, without properly letting consumers know they would automatically be billed in future months.

"When you sign up at a record club they tell you you have to cancel," said David Medine, who heads the credit division of the FTC. "When you signed up for your free trial membership (for the on-line services) they didn't tell you you had to cancel."
Another problem was that consumers would be surprised by automatic debits of their checking accounts for unanticipated amounts of money. That will change.
The companies will have to get proper authorization to debit checking accounts. And that's not all.

"The firms will have to provide a 10-day advance notice of differing debits to checking accounts. If you have a flat fee of $19.95 every month you won't get notice, but if you run up higher or lower charges you will get notice," he said.
The FTC noted in a statement that AOL, based in Dulles, Virginia, is the world's largest online service provider, with eight million customers.
CompuServe, based in Columbus Ohio, is second. Prodigy, based in White Plains, N.Y., is privately held and ranks fourth, after the Microsoft Network.

The FTC said that AOL promised that customer accounts would be debited only after customers returned a written authorization. But AOL actually went ahead and debited the accounts without authorization, the FTC said, in violation of federal law.
The agreement to end the practices will be subject to public comment for 60 days. Comments may be made to the FTC through its Web site at WWW.FTC.GOV, by clicking on "questions or comments."
